title: Two workshops and a trade
context: In a day, workshop A can make 24 shelves or 12 chairs; workshop B can make 12 shelves or 12 chairs. Assume linear frontiers and no transport cost.
prompts: Calculate each workshop’s opportunity cost of a chair.
Identify each comparative advantage.
Propose mutually beneficial terms for one chair.
Explain why consumption gains do not require the production frontier to shift.
criteria: A: 2 shelves per chair; B: 1 shelf per chair.
B has comparative advantage in chairs; A in shelves.
Any strictly intermediate rate, such as 1.5 shelves per chair, benefits both at the margin.
Trade reallocates production and exchange; it expands feasible consumption without changing resources or technology.

title: A taxed competitive market
context: Demand is P = 100 − Q; supply is P = 20 + Q. A tax of 20 is imposed per unit. Assume no externalities and no other changes.
prompts: Draw and label demand, supply and the tax wedge.
Find quantities before and after the tax.
Calculate buyer price, seller price and tax revenue.
Calculate deadweight loss and distinguish it from revenue.
criteria: Before tax: Q = 40, P = 60.
After tax: 100 − Q = 40 + Q, so Q = 30.
Buyer price 70; seller price 50; revenue 20 × 30 = 600.
DWL = ½ × 20 × 10 = 100; revenue is a transfer, while DWL is lost total surplus.

title: Produce or shut down?
context: A price-taking firm’s profit-maximizing operating output is 20. Price is 8, AVC is 6, and ATC is 10. Assume the cost curves are consistent with that output.
prompts: Calculate total revenue and total cost.
Calculate variable cost and fixed cost.
Compare operating profit with shutdown profit.
Explain the long-run implication if price and costs persist with free exit.
criteria: TR = 160 and TC = 200.
Operating profit is −40, versus −80 on shutdown, so operate in the short run.
Persistent inability to cover all economic costs leads to exit in the long run; a short-run loss alone does not require shutdown.

title: A single-price monopoly
context: Demand is P = 80 − Q, MR = 80 − 2Q, MC = 20, and ATC at the chosen output is 30. No externalities are present.
prompts: Find the profit-maximizing output.
Read price from the correct curve.
Calculate profit.
Compare quantity with the allocatively efficient quantity and explain the difference.
criteria: Set MR = MC: Q = 30.
Demand gives P = 50, not 20.
Efficient Q solves demand = MC, giving 60; monopoly restricts output and has P > MC.

title: Hiring at a fixed wage
context: Successive workers’ MRP values are 60, 50, 40, 30 and 20. Wage is fixed at 35. Other costs do not change.
prompts: Choose the profit-maximizing number of workers.
Calculate payroll.
Explain a hiring-demand shift if product price rises in a competitive output market.
Explain why the same wage rule cannot be transferred unchanged to a uniform-wage monopsonist.
criteria: Hire three: each has MRP at least 35; the fourth does not.
Payroll = 3 × 35 = 105.
MRP = MP × P rises at each employment level if MP is unchanged, shifting labor demand right.
A monopsonist faces rising labor supply, so MFC can exceed the wage and hiring uses MRP = MFC.

title: Pricing an external cost
context: Demand/MSB is 100 − Q. MPC is 20 + Q. Constant external damage is 10 per unit. Assume no other distortions.
prompts: Find the uncorrected market quantity.
Find the efficient quantity.
Propose a per-unit corrective tax and explain the mechanism.
Name a measurement challenge and a distributional issue in applying the policy.
criteria: Market Q = 40.
MSC = 30 + Q, so efficient Q = 35.
A tax of 10 aligns private cost with social cost at the efficient quantity.
Damage estimation and monitoring can be difficult; costs and revenue uses affect different groups differently.
